# Edited Nearest Neighbor {#sec-imbalenced-enn}

::: {style="visibility: hidden; height: 0px;"}
## Edited Nearest Neighbor
:::

This method is another undersampling method,
it works by removing observations close to the decision boundary between classes [@wilson1972enn].
This method tries to remove observations that would otherwise be hard to classify.

The algorithm goes as follows:

1. Compute the k nearest neighbors for each observation in the data set.
2. Remove observations from the majority class if the removal criteria are satisfied.

The removal criteria is something we can choose different options for.
A typical implementation will either remove an observation if the majority of the neighbors are of a different class,
but you could also tighten this and remove an observation if any of the neighbors are of a different class.

The idea is that we are able to remove noisy observations this way.
And depending on which criteria you choose, you could see how that would be.
By only allowing us to keep all the observations that have neighbors all of the same class,
we can end up removing a lot of the decision boundary,
especially any area where there is overlap.

The general framework is based on 2 classes,
but we can expand it to a multi-class setting by doing a 1-vs-rest.
This is fairly standard for all of these types of methods.
However, it does change a little bit how things will happen.
In the two-class example,
any majority point deeply embedded in the minority class will most likely be removed.
However, if we are using a multiple-class implementation,
where a single observation from one majority class is deeply embedded into another majority class,
then we will not only delete the single point,
but we will also delete all the points around it that are its neighbors if we use the "any" criterion.
This feels less ideal and is something we have to think about when applying this method.

By itself, this method is simple,
and there have been a couple of method that expands on the foundation of this method.
The first one is **Repeated Edited Nearest Neighbor** [@tomek1976enn].
And it does what it says,
it repeats Edited Nearest Neighbor a number of times.
You can either set it up such that it runs a fixed number of times
or until no observations are removed during an iteration.

Another named variant **AllKNN**.
This is a variant of Edited Nearest Neighbors,
where you select a value of `k`, then apply ENN with neighbors `1` through `k`.
Both of these variants result in more observations being removed.

The last extension we will talk about is the **Neighborhood Cleaning Rule** [@laurikkala2001ncl].
This method starts by running Edited Nearest Neighbor.
Then we run a K Nearest Neighbors on the minority observations.
Any majority class observations that misclassify a minority observation will be removed as well.

## R Examples

```{r}
#| label: ames
#| echo: false
#| message: false
set.seed(1234)
```

We will be using the same subset of the `ames` data set as in the [up-sampling](imbalenced-upsample.qmd) chapter.

```{r}
#| label: show-data
#| message: false
library(recipes)
library(themis)
library(modeldata)
library(dplyr)
data("ames")

ames_imbalance <- ames |>
  filter(MS_Zoning %in% c("Residential_Low_Density", "Residential_Medium_Density")) |>
  mutate(MS_Zoning = droplevels(MS_Zoning)) |>
  select(MS_Zoning, Lot_Area, Year_Built, Gr_Liv_Area, Full_Bath)

ames_imbalance |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

{themis} provides `step_enn()`.
Conveniently, all three of the variants described above are reachable from this one step.

The `kind_sel` argument picks the removal criterion.
The default `"mode"` removes an observation when the majority of its neighbors disagree with it, and `"all"` is the stricter version that removes it unless every neighbor agrees.

```{r}
#| label: step_enn
recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
  step_enn(MS_Zoning, kind_sel = "mode") |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

```{r}
#| label: step_enn-all
recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
  step_enn(MS_Zoning, kind_sel = "all") |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

The stricter criterion removes more, which is what we would expect.

Something else is worth noticing here.
Both classes shrank.
The description above talks about removing observations from the majority class, but this implementation applies the rule to every class.
A minority observation sitting in the middle of the majority class is exactly the kind of point the rule catches, and there is nothing in the rule itself that says to spare it.
If you only want to clean the majority class, that is a choice the implementation has to make for you, and it is worth checking which one yours made.

The `times` argument gives **Repeated Edited Nearest Neighbors** by running the procedure more than once.

```{r}
#| label: step_enn-times
recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
  step_enn(MS_Zoning, times = 3) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

And `all_k` gives **AllKNN**, applying the rule with neighbor counts from 1 up to `neighbors`.

```{r}
#| label: step_enn-all_k
recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
  step_enn(MS_Zoning, all_k = TRUE) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

The **Neighborhood Cleaning Rule** is a separate step, `step_ncl()`.

```{r}
#| label: step_ncl
recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
  step_ncl(MS_Zoning) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

Note that this one left the minority class untouched, unlike `step_enn()` above.
That is by design, since the second stage of the rule is specifically about protecting minority observations.

## Python Examples

```{python}
#| label: python-setup
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
from sklearn import set_config

set_config(transform_output="pandas")
pd.set_option('display.precision', 3)
```

We are using the same subset of the `ames` data set as above.

```{python}
#| label: show-data-py
from feazdata import ames

ames_imbalance = ames[ames["MS_Zoning"].isin(
    ["Residential_Low_Density", "Residential_Medium_Density"])]

X = ames_imbalance[["Lot_Area", "Year_Built", "Gr_Liv_Area", "Full_Bath"]]
y = ames_imbalance["MS_Zoning"]

y.value_counts()
```

Where {themis} reaches the variants through arguments to one step, {imblearn} gives each of them its own class.
`EditedNearestNeighbours()` is the base method.

```{python}
#| label: editednearestneighbours
from imblearn.under_sampling import EditedNearestNeighbours

X_res, y_res = EditedNearestNeighbours(kind_sel="all").fit_resample(X, y)

y_res.value_counts()
```

Note that only the majority class lost observations here, where the {themis} version removed from both.
This is the implementation choice mentioned above, and the two packages made it differently.
The majority class lands on exactly the same count in both, which is a good sign that the disagreement really is only about which classes the rule gets applied to, and not about the rule itself.

`RepeatedEditedNearestNeighbours()` is the repeated variant.

```{python}
#| label: repeatededitednearestneighbours
from imblearn.under_sampling import RepeatedEditedNearestNeighbours

X_res, y_res = RepeatedEditedNearestNeighbours(kind_sel="all").fit_resample(X, y)

y_res.value_counts()
```

And `AllKNN()` is the variant that sweeps over neighbor counts.

```{python}
#| label: allknn
from imblearn.under_sampling import AllKNN

X_res, y_res = AllKNN(kind_sel="all").fit_resample(X, y)

y_res.value_counts()
```

Two things in this chapter cannot be shown running.
`EditedNearestNeighbours(kind_sel="mode")` and `NeighbourhoodCleaningRule()` both raise an error when the outcome is a character or factor column, which is how the class labels are stored throughout this book.
Both work when the labels are integer-coded, which is why the examples above all pass `kind_sel="all"` explicitly.

As with the [instance hardness](imbalenced-hardness-threshold.qmd) chapter, this is a version incompatibility rather than a property of the method.
It comes from a change in {scipy}, which no longer accepts non-numeric input in the routine that computes the mode, and it may well be fixed by the time you read this.
